title: The self right here
hook: six seekers name the self as far-off things, and a king points closer
carry: this self, right here, is brahman
tomorrow: you keep promising to change a habit. where does change start?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed tat tvam asi with Madhva's reading: for him, difference makes devotion possible. Today, a new great saying, and it trades that for this.

You met them once in the Chandogya: six learned men, Uddalaka among them, who went to King Ashvapati with one question. What is our self, and what is Brahman? Before he taught them, the king asked each one: what do you worship as the self? One said the sky. One said the sun. Then the wind, open space, the waters, the earth. Big, far answers, every one. And the king told them: each of you knows a piece, as if the self were somewhere apart.
screen: `WHAT IS OUR SELF?` → `THE SKY. THE SUN. THE EARTH.` → `AS IF IT WERE SOMEWHERE APART.`

segments.voice: Then he joined the pieces. The sky is the head of this self, the sun its eye, the wind its breath, and on down to the earth as its feet. One self, Vaishvanara, the self in everyone, and not somewhere apart from the ones asking. The Mandukya, a short Upanishad about Om, puts that in three words. In paraphrase, near its start: all this is Brahman. This self is Brahman. This self has four quarters. The middle sentence is the great saying: ayam atma brahma. Its force is in the first word. Tat, that, points across a distance. Ayam, this, is the word for what's near: the cup in your hand, not the hill on the horizon. So here's the teaching, said plainly, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest. The atman, your own self, is not apart from Brahman, the reality behind everything. Tradition gives each of the four Vedas one great saying, and this is the Atharva Veda's. The schools explain the 'is' differently, as this week has shown: for some it means the very same, for others Brahman dwelling within you as your inner guide. But none of them sends you to look for the sacred far away. That's why many Hindus explain namaste as a bow to the divine in the person in front of you. And on a day God feels distant, or holiness seems to live only in a temple you can't get to, this saying turns you around: start here. For now, stay with the pointing: this one, right here.
screen: `SKY, SUN, EARTH: ONE SELF.` · `AYAM ATMA BRAHMA: THIS SELF.` · `ATMAN, NOT APART FROM BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `THIS ONE. RIGHT HERE.`

segments.voice: Look at something far away, a window or the wall across the room, and notice the word that fits it: that. Then rest one hand on your chest and feel it rise and fall. With each rise, let the other word come: this. Then, quietly, say the saying a few times: ayam atma brahma. Vedanta students have long sat with the great sayings this way.
Ayam atma brahma: this self is Brahman, with ayam, this, pointing at the self right here.
Your line: this self, right here, is Brahman. Not the far sky, not the far sun: this one. See you tomorrow.
